question: In the 2017 randomized controlled trial of short-term rapamycin in 24 middle-aged companion dogs, which three echocardiographic measures suggested improvement in age-related heart function in the rapamycin-treated dogs?
answer: E/A ratio, fractional shortening, and ejection fraction (covering both diastolic and systolic measures).

evidence.title: A randomized controlled trial to establish effects of short-term rapamycin treatment in 24 middle-aged companion dogs.
evidence.quote: Echocardiography suggested improvement in both diastolic and systolic age-related measures of heart function (E/A ratio, fractional shortening, and ejection fraction) in the rapamycin-treated dogs.

question: In the 2023 masked, placebo-controlled, randomized trial of low-dose rapamycin in 17 healthy client-owned dogs, what rapamycin dose was used, how often was it given, and for how long?
answer: 0.025 mg/kg, administered three times per week for 6 months.

evidence.title: A masked, placebo-controlled, randomized clinical trial evaluating safety and the effect on cardiac function of low-dose rapamycin in 17 healthy client-owned dogs.
evidence.quote: Low-dose rapamycin (0.025 mg/kg) or placebo was administered three times per week for 6 months.

question: In the 2023 placebo-controlled trial of low-dose rapamycin in 17 healthy client-owned dogs, in what percentage of the bi-weekly owner surveys were perceived positive changes in behavior or health reported for rapamycin-treated dogs, compared with placebo-treated dogs?
answer: 26.8% of surveys for rapamycin-treated dogs versus 8.1% for placebo-treated dogs.

evidence.title: A masked, placebo-controlled, randomized clinical trial evaluating safety and the effect on cardiac function of low-dose rapamycin in 17 healthy client-owned dogs.
evidence.quote: In 26.8% of the bi-weekly surveys owners whose dogs received rapamycin reported perceived positive changes in behavior or health, compared to 8.1% in the placebo group

notes: The abstract reports p = 0.04 for this comparison; the p-value is outside the cited span.

question: How is the design of the Test of Rapamycin in Aging Dogs (TRIAD) clinical trial characterised, and from what population are its healthy middle-aged dogs recruited?
answer: A parallel-group, double-masked, randomized, placebo-controlled, multicenter trial; dogs are recruited from Dog Aging Project participants.

evidence.title: Test of Rapamycin in Aging Dogs (TRIAD): study design and rationale for a prospective, parallel-group, double-masked, randomized, placebo-controlled, multicenter trial of rapamycin in healthy middle-aged dogs from the Dog Aging Project.
evidence.quote: The Test of Rapamycin In Aging Dogs (TRIAD) randomized clinical trial is a parallel-group, double-masked, randomized, placebo-controlled, multicenter trial that will test the ability of rapamycin to prolong lifespan and improve several healthspan metrics in healthy, middle-aged dogs recruited from Dog Aging Project participants.

question: In the Test of Rapamycin in Aging Dogs (TRIAD) trial, what oral rapamycin dose and dosing frequency are used, for how long is treatment given, and how long is the post-treatment monitoring period?
answer: 0.15 mg/kg orally once weekly for 12 months, followed by a 24-month post-treatment monitoring period.

evidence.title: Rapamycin as a potential intervention to promote longevity and extend healthspan in companion dogs
evidence.quote: Participants are randomized in a 1:1 ratio to receive rapamycin (0.15 mg/kg PO) or a placebo once weekly for 12 months, followed by a 24-month post-treatment monitoring period.

notes: Grounded in a 2025 review's description of the TRIAD protocol (full text); the TRIAD design paper itself has abstract-only coverage in the corpus.

question: How many dogs in total (and per arm) will be enrolled and randomized in the TRIAD rapamycin trial, and what minimum difference in mean lifespan between treatment groups is the trial powered (at more than 80%) to detect?
answer: 580 dogs (290 rapamycin-treated, 290 placebo-treated); more than 80% power to detect a 6% or greater difference in mean lifespan.

evidence.title: Rapamycin as a potential intervention to promote longevity and extend healthspan in companion dogs
evidence.quote: A total of 580 dogs (n = 290 rapamycin-treated, n = 290 placebo-treated) will be enrolled and randomized, and for the primary outcome measure of survival time from randomization, the trial will have > 80% power to detect a 6% or greater difference in mean lifespan between treatment groups.

question: In the case report of an eight-year-old castrated male Labrador retriever that developed severe asymptomatic hypertriglyceridemia during six months of low-dose rapamycin, how long after rapamycin was discontinued did the lipemia and hypertriglyceridemia resolve, and what lipid-targeted treatment was required?
answer: They completely resolved within 15 days of stopping rapamycin, with no targeted lipemic intervention.

evidence.title: Case report: Severe asymptomatic hypertriglyceridemia associated with long-term low-dose rapamycin administration in a healthy middle-aged Labrador retriever.
evidence.quote: Within 15 days of discontinuing rapamycin treatment, and with no targeted lipemic intervention, the dog's lipemia and hypertriglyceridemia completely resolved.

question: In the lifetime diet restriction study of 48 Labrador retrievers, in which one dog of each pair was fed 25% less than its pair-mate from 8 weeks of age, by how much was median lifespan extended in the diet-restricted dogs?
answer: Median lifespan was 1.8 years longer in the diet-restricted dogs, with delayed onset of late-life diseases, especially osteoarthritis.

evidence.title: Diet restriction and ageing in the dog: major observations over two decades.
evidence.quote: Labrador retrievers (n 48) were paired at age 6 weeks by sex and weight within each of seven litters, and assigned randomly within the pair to control-feeding (CF) or 25 % diet restriction (DR). Feeding began at age 8 weeks. The same diet was fed to all dogs; only the quantity differed. Major lifetime observations included 1.8 years longer median lifespan among diet-restricted dogs, with delayed onset of late life diseases, especially osteoarthritis.

question: In the 2002 paired-feeding study of 25% diet restriction in 48 Labrador Retrievers, how were median life span and maximum life span defined?
answer: Median life span was the age when 50% of the dogs were deceased; maximum life span was the age when 90% of the dogs were deceased.

evidence.title: Effects of diet restriction on life span and age-related changes in dogs.
evidence.quote: Age at onset of chronic disease and median (age when 50% of the dogs were deceased) and maximum (age when 90% of the dogs were deceased) life spans were evaluated.

question: In the longitudinal study of lifetime 25% calorie restriction in 48 Labrador retrievers, were there differences between diet-restricted and control-fed dogs in the prevalence or severity of radiographic and histopathologic elbow osteoarthritis, despite the 1.8-year extension in median lifespan?
answer: No. No differences in prevalence or severity of radiographic or histopathologic elbow OA were found between feeding groups, and the longer-lived restricted dogs showed no additional incremental worsening of elbow disease.

evidence.title: A longitudinal study of the influence of lifetime food restriction on development of osteoarthritis in the canine elbow.
evidence.quote: No differences in prevalence or severity of radiographic and histopathologic elbow OA were found between feeding groups. Diet restriction resulted in a 1.8-year extension in median lifespan but no additional incremental worsening of elbow disease.

question: In the placebo-controlled L-deprenyl (selegiline) survival study in beagles, how many dogs were enrolled, into how many pairs were they allotted, and what oral dose and treatment duration were used?
answer: 82 beagles allotted to 41 pairs; 1 mg/kg L-deprenyl (or placebo) orally once daily for 2 years and 10 weeks.

evidence.title: Treatment with L-deprenyl prolongs life in elderly dogs.
evidence.quote: Eighty two beagle dogs ranging in age from 2.8 to 16.4 years and in weight from 6.3 to 15.8 kg were allotted to 41 pairs and administered placebo or 1 mg/kg L-deprenyl orally once daily for 2 years and 10 weeks.

question: In the L-deprenyl beagle survival study, what proportions of dogs aged 10-15 years at the start of treatment survived to the end of the study in the L-deprenyl and placebo groups, and what did a later meta-analysis conclude when it reanalysed this dog study accounting for age at enrollment and sex?
answer: 12 of 15 (80%) L-deprenyl dogs versus 7 of 18 (39%) placebo dogs (P=0.017); after adjusting for age at enrollment and sex, the survival effect was no longer significant, though power was limited by small sample size.

evidence.title: Treatment with L-deprenyl prolongs life in elderly dogs.
evidence.quote: To assess whether L-deprenyl treatment begun in later life might enhance canine longevity in a fashion similar to that documented in rodents we also examined survival in a subset of elderly dogs who were between the ages of 10 and 15 yrs at the start of tablet administration and who received tablets for at least 6 months. In this subset, dogs in the L-deprenyl group survived longer (p < 0.05) than dogs in the placebo group. Twelve of 15 (80%) dogs in the L-deprenyl group survived to the conclusion of the study, in contrast to only 7 of 18 (39%) of the dogs who received placebo (P=0.017).

evidence.title: L-deprenyl extends lifespan across mammalian species: A meta-analysis of 22 longevity experiments.
evidence.quote: In addition to the meta-analysis, we reanalyzed a dog survival study by Ruehl et al. When accounting for age at enrollment and sex, the study no longer displayed a significant effect on survival, though power was limited by small sample size.

notes: Synthesis across the original 1997 survival study and its 2025 reanalysis.

question: In the longitudinal study in which 48 aged beagles (9-12 years) were assigned to control or antioxidant-fortified food crossed with a control or enriched environment, which group largely accounted for the treatment effects on size discrimination learning and reversal learning after 1 year?
answer: The combined treatment group (antioxidant-fortified food plus behavioral enrichment) largely accounted for the improvements.

evidence.title: Long-term treatment with antioxidants and a program of behavioral enrichment reduces age-dependent impairment in discrimination and reversal learning in beagle dogs.
evidence.quote: Both tasks were also improved by both the fortified food and the behavioral enrichment. However, in both instances the treatment effects largely reflected improved performance in the combined treatment group.

question: In the 90-day prospective, double-blinded, placebo-controlled trial of diets containing medium-chain triglycerides (MCT) plus a Brain Protection Blend (BPB) in 87 client-owned dogs with signs of cognitive dysfunction syndrome, which diet significantly improved all 6 categories of CDS signs, and in how many categories did the control diet improve?
answer: The 6.5% MCT oil + BPB diet improved all 6 categories; the control diet improved in only 4 of 6 categories.

evidence.title: Efficacy of a Therapeutic Diet on Dogs With Signs of Cognitive Dysfunction Syndrome (CDS): A Prospective Double Blinded Placebo Controlled Clinical Study.
evidence.quote: Eighty-seven dogs were randomly enrolled into one of three diet groups with 29 dogs per group: Control, 6.5% MCT oil + BPB (6.5% MCT diet), 9% MCT oil + BPB (9% MCT diet). Diets were fed for a period of 90 days, and each dog's CDS signs were re-evaluated at day 30 and day 90. All 6 categories of the CDS signs were significantly improved (p <0.05) in the dogs given the 6.5% MCT diet at the end of the 90-day study. Control only improved in 4 out 6 categories.

notes: The abstract's inline HTML italics tags are preserved verbatim in the quote because the validator matches the raw abstract text.

question: In the study that treated 17 retired police dogs with allogeneic canine mesenchymal stem cells, nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) or rapamycin, what oral doses of NMN and rapamycin were given and how often, and what happened to the inflammatory factors IL-6 and TNF-α?
answer: 2.5 g/dog NMN and 3 mg/dog rapamycin, each given every 2 days by mouth; the treatments significantly reduced IL-6 and TNF-α levels.

evidence.title: Transcriptomic and intervention evidence reveals domestic dogs as a promising model for anti-inflammatory investigation.
evidence.quote: The other two groups received dosages of 2.5 g/dog NMN (Mills et al., 2016) and 3 mg/dog Rapa every 2 days by oral administration.

evidence.title: Transcriptomic and intervention evidence reveals domestic dogs as a promising model for anti-inflammatory investigation.
evidence.quote: We next treated aged dogs with canine mesenchymal stem cells (cMSCs), nicotinamide mononucleotide, and rapamycin to determine whether and how they responded to the antiaging interventions. The results showed that these treatments can significantly reduce the level of inflammatory factors (IL-6 and TNF-α).

notes: The number of dogs (17) is stated in the full text; rapamycin was given as a fixed 3 mg per-dog dose rather than mg/kg.
